title: Resource smoothing vs resource levelling
blurb: Tell smoothing (within float, end date unchanged) from levelling (within resource limits, end date may move) and know when to use each.
question: Kestrel Housing is refitting an office with only one electrician available. The draft schedule needs two electricians in weeks 2 and 3, and the handover date is fixed. Should the project manager smooth or level the schedule, and what would each do to the end date?

teach.body: Both techniques re-time activities so that resource demand fits what is available. RESOURCE SMOOTHING adjusts activities only within their float, so the end date does not change: it is time-limited. RESOURCE LEVELLING delays activities as far as needed to stay within resource limits, so the end date may be extended: it is resource-limited. In plain English: smoothing protects the date and does what it can; levelling protects the resource limit and lets the date move.

teach.caption: Rewire and Lighting both need the one electrician in weeks 2 and 3. Lighting has 5 weeks of float; the handover in week 8 is fixed.
Read like a resource histogram: the draft peaks above the limit in weeks 2–3 and leaves weeks 7–8 idle. Smoothing spreads the same work evenly.
Lighting moves to weeks 7–8, inside its float. One electrician all the way through and handover still in week 8. But Lighting now has no float left.

teach.h: Second site: levelling moves the end date
teach.caption: Here both electrical jobs were planned side by side in weeks 1–4 with NO float. With one electrician, levelling delays Fire alarm, so Fit-out and handover slip from week 8 to week 12.

rows.label: Use when
values: Date is fixed and float exists
Resources are capped; date can move

children.label: Level
children.sub: Agree the new date via change control

teach.caption: Smoothing is usually tried first because it protects the date. In iterative working, overload is handled by reprioritising the backlog instead.

teach.body: Smoothing keeps the date but uses up float, so more activities become near-critical and the schedule becomes riskier; it may also leave some peaks unresolved. Levelling gives a plan the resources can truly deliver, but a later finish can mean extra cost, later benefits and a change request for the sponsor. Both are mainly linear-schedule techniques, applied to the resource-loaded plan before it is baselined and again when things change.

teach.text: Exam trap: the two are swapped. If the end date must NOT move, the answer is SMOOTHING (within float). If resources are capped and the date CAN move, it is LEVELLING. Also: levelling MAY extend the end date, not 'always', and moving a zero-float activity is never smoothing.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Define smoothing: re-timing activities within float so the end date is unchanged (time-limited).
Define levelling: delaying activities to stay within resource limits, so the end date may move (resource-limited).
Say what each protects: smoothing the date, levelling the resource limit.
Give a limitation: smoothing is capped by float; levelling can delay delivery and benefits.
Apply it: fixed date with float means smooth; capped resources with a flexible date means level.
Smoothing: within float, end date unchanged, time-limited; may not clear every peak.
Levelling: within resource limits, end date may be extended, resource-limited.
Smoothing uses up float, so the schedule becomes riskier.
Levelling needs the date change agreed through change control.
Fixed date plus float: smooth. Capped resources plus flexible date: level.

summary: You can now explain that resource smoothing re-times activities within their float so the end date holds, while resource levelling keeps demand within resource limits even if the end date moves. You can choose between them for a given scenario and explain the trade-offs of each.

A.q: Which statement best defines resource smoothing?
options: Re-timing work within float so the end date holds
Delaying work beyond float to respect resource limits
Adding resources to critical work to finish sooner
Overlapping activities that would normally be in sequence
A.why: Smoothing moves activities only within their float, so resource peaks are reduced without changing the end date.

whyNot.1: Delaying beyond float to respect resource limits is levelling.
whyNot.2: Adding resources to critical activities is crashing.

A.q: Resource levelling is described as 'resource-limited'. What does this mean?
options: The end date is fixed; resource limits may be exceeded
The resource limit is fixed; the end date may move
Resources are limited to internal staff only
Only the critical path activities are changed
A.why: Levelling treats the resource limit as fixed and delays work to stay within it, even if that extends the end date.

whyNot.0: That reverses it: a fixed end date is the smoothing idea, and neither technique sets out to exceed resource limits.
whyNot.2: Resource-limited refers to the quantity available, not whether staff are internal or external.
whyNot.3: Levelling can move any activity, and delaying critical ones is what pushes the end date out.

A.q: What mainly limits how far resource smoothing can reduce resource peaks?
options: The number of roles shown on the OBS
The size of the contingency budget
The number of levels in the WBS
The float available on activities
A.why: Smoothing can only move work within its float. Once float runs out, any further move would change the end date.

whyNot.0: The OBS shows who is involved; it does not limit how activities can be re-timed.
whyNot.1: Contingency funds risk responses; smoothing does not spend money.
whyNot.2: WBS depth affects the detail of planning, not how far work can move without delaying the end.

B.q: On Kestrel Housing's refit, the lighting job (5 weeks' float) clashes with rewiring for the only electrician. Handover is fixed. What should the project manager do?
options: Delay handover until the clash clears
Hire a second electrician straight away
Move lighting later within its float
Book the electrician on both jobs at once
B.why: Lighting has enough float to move after the other electrical work without touching handover: resource smoothing.

whyNot.0: Moving handover is unnecessary when float can absorb the clash, and the date is fixed.
whyNot.1: Extra resource costs money and is not needed when the clash can be smoothed out.
whyNot.3: Double-booking one electrician is the over-allocation the PM needs to remove.

B.q: After smoothing, Kestrel's lighting job has no float left. What is the main consequence?
options: It is now effectively critical
It has been removed from scope
The end date has moved later
It now needs a second sponsor
B.why: With zero float, any slip on lighting now delays handover. Smoothing has made the schedule more sensitive.

whyNot.1: Smoothing re-times work; it never removes it from scope.
whyNot.2: The move stayed inside the float, so handover is unchanged.
whyNot.3: Float has nothing to do with governance roles.

B.q:
Which TWO statements are true of resource levelling?
1) It must never change the end date
2) It works only on critical activities
3) It keeps demand within resource limits
4) It may delay activities beyond their float
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: Levelling keeps demand within limits (3) and may delay work beyond float to do so (4), which can extend the end date.

whyNot.0: Neither is true: levelling may change the end date and can move any activity.
whyNot.1: Statement 3 is true, but 'never change the end date' describes smoothing.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is true, but levelling is not restricted to critical activities.

C.q: At Kestrel's second site, the rewiring and fire-alarm jobs are both critical and only one electrician can be found. The sponsor accepts the date may move. Which technique fits, and with what effect?
options: Smoothing: fire alarm moved, handover kept
Fast-tracking: jobs overlapped, handover kept
Levelling: fire alarm delayed, handover later
Smoothing: both jobs shortened, handover later
C.why: With no float, staying within one electrician means delaying a critical job, so the end date moves: resource levelling.

whyNot.0: Both jobs are critical with no float, so smoothing cannot move either without changing the date.
whyNot.1: Overlapping the jobs would need two electricians at once, the very constraint that cannot be met.
whyNot.3: Smoothing never extends the end date, and re-timing does not shorten jobs.

C.q: A project manager smooths a schedule, but one resource peak remains on a critical activity. The contract date cannot move. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Level the schedule and move the date
Consider extra resource or re-scoping
Accept the overload and take no action
Smooth again until the peak disappears
C.why: Smoothing has reached the limit of float and levelling would breach the fixed date, so the PM looks at more resource, crashing or a scope change, escalating as needed.

whyNot.0: Levelling would extend the end date, which the contract does not allow.
whyNot.2: Ignoring over-allocation leads to errors, fatigue and slippage.
whyNot.3: Smoothing cannot go further once float is used up on that activity.

C.q: A sponsor asks why levelling moved the finish date when smoothing had not. Which is the best explanation?
options: Levelling ignores the logic between the tasks
Smoothing adds people, so the date is kept
Smoothing only works on critical activities
Levelling holds resource limits beyond float
C.why: Levelling treats the resource limit as fixed and will delay work past its float, so the end date can move. Smoothing stops at the float.

whyNot.0: Levelling respects dependencies; it changes timing, not logic.
whyNot.1: Smoothing re-times work; adding resources is crashing.
whyNot.2: The reverse: smoothing works on activities that HAVE float, so not critical ones.

reteach.title: One hairdresser on the wedding morning
reteach.question: A bride and three bridesmaids all want their hair done by the one hairdresser before an 11am ceremony. How is smoothing different from levelling here?

blocks.h: Shuffle the slots, or move the ceremony?
blocks.body: The plan had two people booked in the same hour. SMOOTHING: the bridesmaids who are ready early slide into free slots, the bride keeps her fixed slot, and the 11am ceremony stays put. That works only while there are spare slots (float). If there is no spare slot, LEVELLING keeps to one hairdresser and pushes the last appointment back, which means the ceremony starts late.

blocks.text: Smoothing protects the ceremony time; levelling protects the hairdresser's limit of one chair and may make the ceremony late.

explain.body: When a resource-loaded schedule asks for more of a resource in a period than is available, that resource is over-allocated. A histogram shows it as a peak above the limit. Smoothing and levelling are the two techniques that re-time work to remove or reduce those peaks.

test.q: Why might a project manager apply smoothing or levelling to a draft schedule?
options: To remove resource over-allocation
To decompose scope into work packages
To give each package one accountable
To work out the project's earned value
test.why: Both techniques re-time activities so that resource demand fits the resources available.

whyNot.2: Assigning accountability is done with a RACI.
whyNot.3: Earned value measures performance against the baseline.

explain.body: Smoothing moves non-critical activities within their float to flatten peaks. The end date is fixed (time-limited), so if float runs out, some overload may remain. Float that is used up makes the schedule more fragile.

test.q: Which change is an example of resource smoothing?
options: Delaying a critical task by two weeks
Moving a non-critical task within float
Adding two weeks to the planned end date
Cutting one deliverable from the scope
test.why: Moving non-critical work within its float reduces peaks without affecting the end date.

whyNot.0: A critical task has no float, so delaying it moves the end date: not smoothing.
whyNot.2: Smoothing keeps the end date fixed.
whyNot.3: Removing scope is a change request, not smoothing.

explain.body: Levelling treats the resource limit as fixed and delays activities, beyond their float if necessary, until demand fits (resource-limited). Every peak is removed, but the end date may be extended, which needs agreeing through change control.

test.q: What is the main risk of applying resource levelling?
options: Resource limits will be exceeded
Float appears on the critical path
The end date may be extended
The RACI loses its accountable
test.why: Levelling may delay work beyond its float, which can push out the end date and delay benefits.

whyNot.0: Levelling exists precisely to keep within resource limits.
whyNot.1: Levelling tends to consume float, not create it on the critical path.

explain.body: Ask two questions. Is the end date fixed? Is there float where the peaks are? Fixed date with float: smooth first. Capped resources and a date that can move: level. Fixed date, no float: neither works alone, so look at extra resource, crashing, re-scoping or escalation.

rows.label: Fixed contract date, peaks on tasks with float
Only two specialists exist, date can slip
Fixed date, peak on a zero-float task

test.q: The end date is fixed and the over-allocated activities all have plenty of float. Which technique should be tried first?
options: Resource levelling
Crashing the schedule
Re-baselining the plan
Resource smoothing
test.why: Plenty of float and a fixed date are exactly the conditions smoothing is designed for.

whyNot.0: Levelling may move the end date, which is fixed here.
whyNot.1: Crashing adds cost and is unnecessary when float can absorb the peaks.
whyNot.2: Re-baselining is for approved changes, not a first response to resource peaks.
